summary:
Solomon Islands criminalises consensual same-sex sexual activity between men and between women under colonial-era Penal Code provisions, carrying a maximum penalty of 14 years' imprisonment. The ILGA World Database and the Human Dignity Trust both record the offence and the same statutory maximum, and both attribute it to the colonial legal inheritance.

No prosecutions are recorded. US State Department human rights reporting for 2010, 2011, 2012 and 2013 found no arrests or prosecutions directed at LGBT people, and the Human Dignity Trust profile documents an absence of recorded prosecutions in recent years. The offence nonetheless stands, so a visitor's exposure rests on the statute remaining on the books rather than on an active prosecution campaign.

There is no protective framework. No relationship recognition exists for same-sex couples, no non-discrimination shield covers sexual orientation or gender identity, and Parliament has not legislated a same-sex marriage law. Monitoring bodies record no LGBT-specific abuses and no abuses by security forces in the reporting years covered, which places practical risk in the criminal provision itself, in social responses, and in the absence of legal protection.

Official hostility is stated and repeated. The Law Reform Commission proposed legalising gay and lesbian sexual activity in December 2008, the proposal was strongly opposed, and the government told the United Nations in 2011 that it had no intention of decriminalising homosexuality. Prime Minister Manasseh Sogavare publicly opposed same-sex marriage in a 2017 speech to a local church group. In June 2018 Governor General Sir Frank Kabui used his Queen's Birthday address to warn that 'same sex marriage cannot populate the world', while also acknowledging that being gay or lesbian is said to be biological and beyond individual control, and still condemning legal change on the authority of both the criminal code and the Bible.

Constitutional protection was drafted and then withdrawn. A 2009 draft constitution listed sexual orientation as a prohibited ground of discrimination; the 2011, 2013 and 2014 drafts dropped it, and reform remained ongoing as of 2019. The trajectory runs toward narrowing visibility rather than toward repeal.
tangentialFactors:
US State Department reporting for 2011 and 2013 records violence and discrimination against women as prevalent, and the 2011 report describes lengthy pretrial detention and corruption in the justice system. None of these are trans-specific, but they describe the courts and detention facilities a visitor would enter if the sex-offence provisions were ever used.

The 2010 report is framed around the Regional Assistance Mission to Solomon Islands (RAMSI) and the Lusibaea case as markers of general human-rights conditions. That baseline describes a post-intervention governance setting with a strong external security presence during the reporting period.

Criminalisation for both men and women is relatively uncommon among Pacific jurisdictions, so the statutory exposure here is broader than a male-only offence would be, and the absence of enforcement has been consistent across a decade of reporting rather than a single-year finding.
localsOnly:
Residents live under the Penal Code provisions with no statutory protection on sexual orientation or gender identity in employment, housing, services or education, and no means of registering a partnership. Repeated government statements, including the 2011 communication to the United Nations, indicate that decriminalisation is not on the legislative agenda.

Constitutional reform is the only route by which sexual orientation could re-enter the text as a prohibited ground, and the drafts from 2011 onward removed it. Reform remained unresolved as of 2019, so residents have no enforceable constitutional argument on that ground in the current draft framework.

Public statements by the head of government and the head of state frame same-sex relationships as contrary to both statute and Christian teaching. Open advocacy carries the reputational cost of contradicting stated national position in addition to any social response.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve whether gender identity or trans status is addressed anywhere in Solomon Islands law, whether legal gender recognition exists, or whether any screening, medical or documentation rule applies to a trans visitor. No source in the inventory covers those questions, and none should be inferred from the same-sex conduct provisions.

Whether the 14-year maximum has ever been sought or considered in a specific case is not sourced; the record shows no prosecutions for 2010 through 2013 and no recorded prosecutions in recent years, but post-2013 enforcement data is not available in this inventory.

Facilities, access to gender-affirming care, and any entry or visa screening that could disclose trans status are unresolved on these sources. The status of constitutional reform after 2019 is likewise not sourced here.
